thread.title: Apple has its problems but the App Store isn’t one of them, says Bernstein

author: Emily Bary
title: Apple has its problems but the App Store isn’t one of them, says Bernstein
text:
Apple Inc. shares have lost more than a quarter of their value over the past three months, amid concerns about iPhone sales, China demand, and trade-war headwinds, but Bernstein analyst Toni Sacconaghi said there’s at least one issue that investors shouldn’t be worried about.
“We are not concerned – at all – about potential disintermediation of the App Store,” he wrote in a Friday note to clients. “It’s not a top concern of ours. In fact, it’s not even a top seven concern.”
His comments in defense of the App Store’s business model come as several popular tech companies have talked about pulling back on the ways they use this Apple AAPL, +0.50% platform. In particular, Netflix Inc. NFLX, -3.97% Spotify Technology SA SPOT, -0.29% and the makers of Fortnite have complained about the “Apple tax” that shaves 15% to 30% off their App Store revenue when consumers sign up for a subscription inside one of their apps, or buy an app outright.
Don’t miss: Apple’s Tim Cook says regulatory action is needed to restore ‘full faith’ in tech
The App Store has been a star of Apple’s fast-growing services segment , bringing in revenue when users make various app-related purchases, but some investors have added the longevity of this model to their laundry list of fears about the company. Sacconaghi, however, said the “revolt” by these big developers and publishers is “dead on arrival.”
During Apple’s latest earnings call, Chief Financial Officer Luca Maestri said that the highest-grossing app in the App Store constitutes “less than 0.3%” of services revenue, which equates to about 0.04% of the company’s overall revenue for the 2018 fiscal year.
“0.3% is… not a lot of money,” he wrote. “And as a reminder, just because Netflix has left the ecosystem doesn’t mean the $110 million goes away for Apple. Instead, everybody who is a current Netflix subscriber via iOS will continue to pay Apple their ~15% cut. Apple simply won’t receive incremental revenues from Netflix going forward.”
Apple is clearly positioning services revenue as something it wants investors to pay closer attention to, especially given weakening trends for its iPhone business; the company announced on its last earnings call that it would henceforth stop reporting unit-sales figures for its various hardware categories but that it would also be slightly more forthcoming with the information it provides about services.
Opinion: Apple lives up to Wall Street’s fears with massive revenue shortfall
Sacconaghi said he’s not sure whether future legal actions or court rulings will seek to upend the App Store’s dominance, but he’s not panicking just yet: “Could every iOS app take the Fortnite route? Could competing app stores pop up? If you really think about it, you’ll realize… probably not.”
That’s not to say Sacconaghi doesn’t have other worries about the Services business, however. “Worry what you will about the iPhone, or even about Services (we ourselves have previously pointed out headwinds such as slowing installed base growth, tough comps on licensing, and China exposure),” he wrote. “But let’s give Apple some credit—the fundamental business behind the App Store is going to be just fine.”
He has a market perform rating on the shares and a $160 price target. Apple’s stock has gained 1% in Friday trading, and it’s dropped 27% over the past three months. The Dow Jones Industrial Average DJIA, +1.17% has dropped 2.6% in that time.
Emily Bary Emily Bary is a MarketWatch reporter based in New York.
